The phone's bottom bar is written down, with the numbers measured on the app that has one rather than reasoned out in advance.

## ✨ Added

- **A new section, "The bottom bar (the phone's rail)".** On a phone the rail becomes a bar along the bottom, because a rail is reachable with a mouse and a bar is reachable with a thumb. Same job as the sidebar, same `aria-current="page"` semantics, different reach. Eleven rules, each one settled on a shipping app rather than in advance.
- **The rule that pays for the section: the bar is a card inset from every edge, and the mechanism is not the obvious one.** The bar itself goes transparent and the card is drawn behind it. That is the only way the card can be inset while the bar still reserves its full height from the screen above. Give the bar margins instead and it shifts its own glyphs while leaving the reserved space standing.
- **A fixed height, not a floor, and the number is measured.** It started at `min-height: 44`, which every label mode cleared except text-and-glyph: that one measures a glyph, a gap, a caption line and the padding, lands a couple of points over, and the bar grew by exactly that much. A strip at the bottom edge that changes height when a SETTING changes reads as the page having moved. 48 is the tallest case: 20 for the glyph, 2 for the gap, the caption's line, 5 above and below.
- **It paints the app's own ground.** Android's window background is near-white and showed through around the inset card, measured at `#fafafa` beside a page in `#161616`.
- **One stack per tab, never one across the app.** Android's back gesture is a promise about where you came from, and a single stack breaks it the first time somebody switches tabs mid-task. A tab that goes nowhere is still a stack of one, so it is built like the others and gets a header that says what it is.
- **If the main pages should swipe sideways, the bar is a top tab bar moved to the bottom.** A bottom-tab navigator cannot swipe between its pages and a top-tab navigator can, and nothing else changes when its bar is positioned at the bottom. Worth knowing before building the bar twice.

## 🎨 Design

- **A surface that exists in one app and not in the reference gets its own label axis rather than borrowing one.** The bottom bar is the case that established it: it is the only control always on screen and the only one carrying four or five words at phone width, so its trade between space and clarity is its own. The axis defaults to following the app-wide setting, so nothing moves for somebody who never opens it.
- **The reference still declares three axes, and that is deliberate.** The web surface has no bottom bar, and an axis nothing consumes is worse than no axis. An app that has a bar adds the fourth itself.
- **The bar carries no label-mode selector of its own.** The control that sets a mode does not live in the surface it changes.
- **The current tab is filled, never coloured text.** Accent-coloured text is how a link looks, and in this language what is selected is filled. The difference is visible from across a room.
- **Measure the thing you are copying in the app you are copying it into.** One app caps its settings cards to the measured width of its own tab strip. Copied literally into an app whose bar has three tabs instead of seven, that yields a 230px column and every selector inside it stands vertical.
